# Background
Literature published in peer-reviewed papers specifically estimating the local economic impacts of data centers is extremely limited. Consequently, we expand our scope to include preprint sources, such as those published on the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), and personal publications by academics. This expanded search yields two key papers: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry by Yue and Zeng[@Yue2026], and Data Centers and Local Job Creation by Hicks[@Hicks2025].

Yue and Zeng use data center data sourced from Aterio and run difference-in-differences analyses, splitting their data into rural and metropolitan-classified counties. They test the impact of a county receiving its first data center on employment, wages, business establishment count, median household income, unemployment rates, building permits, and electricity prices. Five years after a county receives a data center, the authors find statistically significant increases in employment (+3.5%), wages (+5.0%), business establishments (+4.7%), median household income (+1.9%), and housing construction permits (+16%). The effect on unemployment was statistically insignificant, and the impacts on electricity prices were difficult to interpret. The effects on employment, wages, and business establishments were found to be significant in metro counties but not in rural ones. Conversely, non-metro counties showed a significant decline in unemployment rates that was not present in metro counties.

Hicks’s paper[@Hicks2025] looks only at data centers in Texas and does not make a distinction between rural and urban counties. Like Yue and Zeng[@Yue2026], he leverages difference-in-differences models to test the impact of data center entry into a county on local economic variables. Hicks’s analysis window covers only eight quarters, or two years, before and after the treatment event, which could hide impacts that take longer to materialize. Overall, this paper does not find substantial impacts on labor markets, with the potential exception of very large-scale AI data centers. It does find a short-term boost in construction immediately after a data center enters a county, which quickly fades.

In addition to the standard economic outcomes analyzed by Hicks[@Hicks2025] and Yue and Zeng[@Yue2026], we research potential environmental variables that can be incorporated directly into an economic framework. Due to data availability limitations, we narrow our environmental scope to include only air quality. Unlike local economic impacts, the environmental impacts of data centers are more well-studied. The Cloud Next Door: Investigating the Environmental and Socioeconomic Strain of Datacenters on Local Communities by Ngata et al.[@Ngata2025] highlights that nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$​) and fine particulate matter ($\text{PM}_{2.5}$​) are the primary air pollutants associated with data centers and proposes that a mix of on-site diesel backup power generators and induced power demand on fossil-fuel power plants are the main mechanism by which data centers cause air pollution. Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers by Han et al.[@Han2024] also links data centers to increases in $\text{NO}_x$​ and $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ air pollution, as well as sulfur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$​), and estimates the economic costs associated with negative health outcomes. Estimating the Health and Economic Impacts of Changes in Local Air Quality by Carvour et al.[@Carvour2018] goes further by estimating the dollar value associated with lower work productivity caused by marginal changes in air pollution. Among air-quality measures, only fine particulate matter ($\text{PM}_{2.5}$) was available as a sufficiently complete county-level dataset across our full study period; comparable data for nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$) and sulfur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) were not sufficiently complete for inclusion.

## Data Sourcing & Organization
Our data sources are split into two groups: primary, from which we derive our primary analytical features, and secondary, which provide supporting information for the primary data. We have seven primary data sources: the Centers of Disease Control (CDC) for air quality, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for unemployment, the National Cancer Institute for population, Data.gov for construction permits, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) for gross domestic product (GDP) and personal income, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) for data centers, and the Census Bureau for business statistics. Augmenting our primary sources, we have three supporting sources: the Census Bureau for county sizes, NAICS code definitions, and Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) codes; California Health and Human Services for county centroids; and Plotly Sample Datasets for mapping county borders. (Additional information and links for all sources can be found in Table A.1 of the Appendix.)

All primary sources were selected because they met both our time criteria of covering at least 2007 to 2022 and our granularity criteria of including data at the county level for all states in the contiguous U.S. All primary datasets already use the Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) code system to uniquely identify counties, naturally making a combination of year and county FIPS code the primary composite key for most of our database tables. For datasets that include NAICS codes, the primary key is a composite of NAICS code, year, and county code.

## Database Design
We store cleaned data in a PostgreSQL database. To avoid unnecessary costs and complexity, we decided against hosting it on a cloud service. Instead, we wrote a database creation script in Python and committed it to our repository. This allowed each team member to recreate the database locally, and if changes are made on one machine, others rerun the script to sync their local copy of the database.

The database is designed to comply with Third Normal Form, which balances data integrity and ease of access. Every table contains a primary key, implemented as a composite key using combinations of year, county ID, and NAICS code, depending on the table.

Our primary tables are stored in the public schema, which is depicted in @fig-erd-schema. After initializing our primary tables, we create copies within a separate schema called “transformed” inside the database. In this schema, we calculate and store spatial calculation versions for all relevant columns, which will be explained further in the methods section. Maintaining separate schemas allows us to maintain idempotency so that we can alter the primary tables as needed without causing dependency issues in our transformed tables.

from graphviz import Digraph
from IPython.display import SVG, display

def entity_label(title, fields):
    rows = [
        "<TR><TD BGCOLOR='#e7dcff' COLSPAN='3' ALIGN='CENTER'><B>"
        + title +
        "</B></TD></TR>"
    ]
    for data_type, field_name, key in fields:
        rows.append(
            "<TR>"
            f"<TD ALIGN='LEFT'>{data_type}</TD>"
            f"<TD ALIGN='LEFT'>{field_name}</TD>"
            f"<TD ALIGN='LEFT'>{key}</TD>"
            "</TR>"
        )
    return (
        "<<TABLE BORDER='1' CELLBORDER='1' CELLSPACING='0' CELLPADDING='3' COLOR='#7c5cc4'>"
        + "".join(rows)
        + "</TABLE>>"
    )

dot = Digraph("county_erd", format="svg", engine="dot")

dot.attr(
    rankdir="TB",
    bgcolor="transparent",
    pad="0.01",
    margin="0",
    nodesep="0.12",
    ranksep="0.32",
    splines="ortho",
)

dot.attr("node", shape="plain", fontname="Arial", fontsize="11")
dot.attr("edge", color="#64748b", penwidth="0.9", arrowsize="0.55", arrowhead="none")


# Table nodes
dot.node("us_counties", label=entity_label("us_counties", [

]))

]))

# vertical stacking within columns
dot.edge("gdp", "population", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("population", "res_construction_permits", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("res_construction_permits", "naics_518_establishments", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("naics_518_establishments", "naics_code_look_up", style="invis", weight="150")

dot.edge("us_counties", "C1", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("C1", "C2", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("C2", "C3", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("C3", "business_patterns", style="invis", weight="150")

dot.edge("unemployment", "personal_income", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("personal_income", "air_quality", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("air_quality", "county_distances_lookup", style="invis", weight="150")
dot.edge("county_distances_lookup", "naics_518_nearby_estabs_50mi", style="invis", weight="150")


# True relationships
for child_table in [
    "population",
    "personal_income",
    "gdp",
    "res_construction_permits",
    "unemployment",
    "air_quality",
    "naics_518_establishments",
    "business_patterns",
    "county_distances_lookup",
    "naics_518_nearby_estabs_50mi",
]:
    dot.edge("us_counties", child_table)

dot.edge("naics_code_look_up", "business_patterns")
dot.edge("naics_518_establishments", "naics_518_nearby_estabs_50mi")
dot.edge("county_distances_lookup", "naics_518_nearby_estabs_50mi")

display(SVG(dot.pipe(format="svg")))

## Data Cleaning
Across our analysis window, our primary datasets posed challenges involving geographic boundary mismatches, timeline classification shifts, sporadic establishment reporting gaps, and localized missingness in environmental records.

Our initial quality checks uncovered persistent inconsistencies in county FIPS codes due to boundary changes, splits, and reclassifications in Virginia and Connecticut. Virginia contains independent cities that lie entirely within a surrounding parent county. When a data source reported separate statistics for an independent city and its parent county, we aggregated those figures and assigned the combined total to the parent county. This standardized our data to match the coarser granularity used by sources that already pre-aggregate those regions. 

For isolated independent cities located outside Virginia, we used a similar methodology, identifying the primary surrounding county and attributing the independent city's data directly to that surrounding county. In 2022, Connecticut officially retired its historical county system in favor of new planning regions with completely redrawn geographic boundaries. Because the 2022 boundaries no longer aligned with historical data, we dropped the reported 2022 values for Connecticut and handled that final year using imputation.

Addressing missingness and temporal consistency required distinct imputation strategies across datasets. Because an open source, historical dataset tracking precise data center locations and construction dates was unavailable, we utilized the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) establishment counts under NAICS code 518 (Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services). While our other sources spanned 2001 through 2022, we restricted our timeline to start in 2007, the last major revision year for the NAICS 518 classification, to ensure the code consistently identified the same establishment type across years.

Within this timeframe, certain counties exhibited sporadic missing records where 518 establishments existed prior to and following an intervening gap. Because the QCEW explicitly records true zero values for counties without qualifying establishments, we treated these omitted intermediate records as reporting gaps rather than closures. We applied linear interpolation across the gap between the last known active year and the subsequent reporting year, flagged all imputed values in our data center table, and assumed boundary values were zero when missingness occurred at the start or end of our timeframe. 

For air quality data, where 46 counties previously present began reporting missing values from 2020 onward, we implemented a spatial fill function based on inverse distance weighting. For any missing county in a given year, the function calculates a distance-weighted average of air quality using the centroids of its five nearest neighboring counties to impute values through the end of the analysis period.

To systematically execute these solutions, we conducted all data cleaning in Python to maintain consistency with our downstream modeling pipeline. We created an individual Python cleaning script for each distinct primary data source to import raw CSV files, execute the geographic aggregations and missingness imputations, standardize data types, remove duplicate rows, and handle necessary transformations. The scripts then use SQLAlchemy to ingest the cleaned data directly into designated PostgreSQL tables. Finally, we execute a series of SQL data quality checks to verify that every row across all tables uniquely joins to the central U.S. Counties Table, ensure there are no duplicate rows, and confirm that each table contains the exact expected county count. If unmatched or unexpected counties appear, we trace these issues back to the source-specific Python cleaning script, apply corrections, re-ingest the data, and rerun the SQL verification queries iteratively until no mismatches remain.
